contentHtml:
Every meaningful action needs a clear relationship between user intent, the system's actual state and the visible result. Design that relationship before connecting a button to an API.

Action Contract

For each consequential action, capture:

Actor and permission:
Label and object/scope:
Prerequisites:
Expected effect and persistence point:
Immediate feedback:
Pending, completed, failed and unknown states:
Duplicate and concurrent-action behavior:
Recovery, cancellation or undo:
Next step and durable confirmation, if needed:

This is a local engineering convention. It connects the visibility and control heuristics in NN/G's usability guidance to implementable behavior.

State Coverage

State What the user needs Required behavior
Loading What is being retrieved Stable layout, progress indication and failure path
Empty Why there is no content yet Appropriate first action
No matches Which search/filter produced no results Clear or adjust filters
Read-only or restricted What is possible with current access Explanation and supported next step
Invalid input What to correct Field context, retained values and correction path
Saving Whether the request is still pending Visible status and duplicate-action control
Completed What changed Confirmed result and relevant next action
Failed What did not complete Accurate explanation and safe recovery
Outcome unknown Whether the change might have succeeded Status reconciliation before unsafe retry
Conflict Which state changed elsewhere Review and reconcile without silent overwrite
Session expired How to regain access Appropriate input preservation and return to task

Use the states that apply to the workflow. Loading or an error is not an empty dataset; do not show No customers yet while a request has failed.

Saving And Truthful Completion

The interface MUST report saved or completed state only after the relevant system has confirmed it. An accepted background request means queued or processing, not finished.

  • Show immediate acknowledgment and meaningful waiting status.
  • Keep submitted values visible while a request is pending.
  • Restore a usable control state after failure.
  • Give long operations a status location that survives navigation when needed.
  • Announce important status changes accessibly without stealing focus.
  • Use durable confirmation for consequential results, with the relevant object or reference and next steps. A short-lived toast may supplement it.

Completion guidance is informed by GOV.UK confirmation pages.

Retry And Unknown Outcome

A network timeout may occur after the server committed a change. The local standard requires the UI and server contract to account for this ambiguity.

For record creation, payments or sending messages, use a supported operation identifier, idempotency mechanism or reconciliation lookup before retrying. Do not assert failure simply because the browser did not receive a response.

Example message when accurate:

We could not confirm whether the customer was created.
Check the operation status before creating it again.

The status route must actually exist and be accessible. Disabling a button prevents some repeated clicks; it does not handle retries, multiple tabs or concurrent requests. Coordinate with Architecture: State, Reliability and Scale.

Explicit Save And Autosave

Use explicit save as a simple default for record forms. Autosave may fit continuous editing when users can understand its scope and undo behavior.

If autosave is used, expose unsaved, saving, saved and failed states; define when persistence happens, handle overlapping changes and provide recovery. Make it clear that navigating away is not a cancellation of already saved changes. Keep destructive or externally visible actions explicit.

When leaving an explicit-save form, warn about meaningful unsaved changes. Do not warn on an unchanged form or an ordinary successful navigation. Browser unload warnings are not a durable draft strategy and may not run reliably.

Delete, Archive And Undo

  • Name the actual effect: archive, deactivate, remove access or delete.
  • Identify the affected object and explain material downstream effects.
  • Offer undo when reversal truly exists, with its time limit and scope.
  • Use review/confirmation for costly or irreversible consequences.
  • Put the action name on the confirming control, not only Yes or OK.
  • Give cancellation a clear path and avoid initial focus on a destructive confirmation by default.

Do not require a confirmation dialog for every routine save. The WCAG error prevention criterion allows several approaches for covered transactions, including reversal, error checking or review before commitment. WCAG error prevention

Conflicts And Partial Success

When a record changes during editing, preserve the user's work and show the latest authoritative state or a supported comparison path. Avoid silently overwriting either version. State who or what changed it only when known and permitted to disclose.

For batch actions, report successes and failures separately. A result such as 8 customers archived; 2 could not be archived must identify a supported way to inspect or retry the failed items without repeating completed effects.

Error Copy

Explain the situation, whether work was preserved and the next possible action. Use a reference identifier when it helps support; keep stack traces, secrets and sensitive implementation details out of the message.

Never show a retry, undo, cancellation or support promise that the product cannot fulfill. Keep essential recovery available after a toast disappears.
